questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the primary purpose of the transport layer (Layer 4)?
questions.option_a: Routing packets between different networks
questions.option_b: Delivering data between application processes on different hosts
questions.option_c: Converting domain names into IP addresses
questions.option_d: Encrypting all transmitted application data
questions.explanation: The transport layer provides end-to-end delivery between processes. IP delivers packets between hosts, while Layer 4 uses port numbers to identify the correct application.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five mandatory tasks shared by TCP and UDP?
questions.option_a: Segmentation
questions.option_b: Multiplexing and demultiplexing
questions.option_c: Congestion control
questions.option_d: Basic error detection
questions.explanation: Congestion control is an additional TCP capability. The five shared tasks include segmentation, multiplexing and demultiplexing, end-to-end process delivery, and basic error detection.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of segmentation at the transport layer?
questions.option_a: To divide application data into transportable units
questions.option_b: To assign IP addresses to individual applications
questions.option_c: To encrypt data before transmission
questions.option_d: To determine the shortest network route
questions.explanation: Segmentation divides application data into smaller transportable units that can be passed down to the network layer.

questions.question: How do port numbers support multiplexing and demultiplexing?
questions.option_a: They identify the physical network interface
questions.option_b: They determine the encryption algorithm
questions.option_c: They replace destination IP addresses
questions.option_d: They allow multiple applications to share an IP address and direct received data to the correct process
questions.explanation: Port numbers distinguish application processes, allowing multiple applications to communicate through the same host IP address.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between IP and Layer 4 delivery?
questions.option_a: IP guarantees delivery to the correct application
questions.option_b: IP provides host-to-host delivery, while Layer 4 provides process-to-process delivery
questions.option_c: Layer 4 performs all network routing
questions.option_d: IP and Layer 4 perform identical delivery functions
questions.explanation: IP identifies the destination host, while the transport layer uses port numbers to deliver data to the appropriate application process.

questions.question: Which error-detection mechanism is present in both TCP and UDP according to the lecture?
questions.option_a: Acknowledgment numbers
questions.option_b: Retransmission timers
questions.option_c: Checksum fields
questions.option_d: Sliding windows
questions.explanation: Both TCP and UDP include checksum fields for basic error detection.

questions.question: Which combination represents capabilities added by TCP beyond the mandatory Layer 4 tasks?
questions.option_a: Connection establishment, reliability, ordering, flow control and congestion control
questions.option_b: IP routing, encryption, authentication and fragmentation
questions.option_c: DNS resolution, addressing and packet forwarding
questions.option_d: Segmentation, multiplexing, checksums and process delivery only
questions.explanation: TCP adds five major capabilities: connection establishment and termination, reliability, ordered delivery, flow control and congestion control.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of TCP acknowledgments?
questions.option_a: To assign destination port numbers
questions.option_b: To encrypt transmitted segments
questions.option_c: To prevent all forms of packet interception
questions.option_d: To confirm received data and support retransmission when data is lost
questions.explanation: Acknowledgments allow TCP to track successful reception and retransmit data that has not been acknowledged.

questions.question: Which TCP mechanism prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver?
questions.option_a: Congestion control
questions.option_b: Flow control
questions.option_c: Port filtering
questions.option_d: Sequence-number randomization
questions.explanation: TCP flow control uses a sliding window to regulate how much data a sender can transmit before receiving acknowledgments.

questions.question: Which TCP mechanism adjusts the transmission rate in response to network conditions?
questions.option_a: Multiplexing
questions.option_b: Flow control
questions.option_c: Congestion control
questions.option_d: Demultiplexing
questions.explanation: Congestion control adjusts TCP's sending rate to reduce network congestion and protect the network.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares TCP and UDP connection establishment?
questions.option_a: TCP requires a three-way handshake, while UDP has no connection-establishment handshake
questions.option_b: Both require a three-way handshake
questions.option_c: UDP requires a four-way handshake
questions.option_d: Neither protocol supports communication without application authentication
questions.explanation: TCP establishes a connection through a three-way handshake. UDP sends datagrams without protocol-level connection establishment.

questions.question: What is the minimum TCP header size and the UDP header size stated in the lecture?
questions.option_a: TCP 8 bytes, UDP 20 bytes
questions.option_b: TCP 16 bytes, UDP 12 bytes
questions.option_c: TCP 40 bytes, UDP 20 bytes
questions.option_d: TCP 20 bytes, UDP 8 bytes
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies TCP's minimum header as 20 bytes and UDP's header as 8 bytes.

questions.question: Which application category is most suitable for UDP according to the lecture?
questions.option_a: Reliable file transfer
questions.option_b: Latency-sensitive, loss-tolerant communication such as VoIP and gaming
questions.option_c: Applications requiring guaranteed ordered delivery
questions.option_d: Applications requiring automatic retransmission of every lost segment
questions.explanation: UDP's low overhead makes it suitable for latency-sensitive applications that can tolerate some packet loss.

questions.question: What is a socket?
questions.option_a: A physical connection between two network devices
questions.option_b: An encryption key assigned to a network connection
questions.option_c: A communication endpoint identified by an IP address and a port number
questions.option_d: A routing table entry containing a destination network
questions.explanation: A socket is a communication endpoint represented by an IP address paired with a port number.

questions.question: Which four values uniquely identify a TCP connection according to the lecture?
questions.option_a: Source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port
questions.option_b: Source MAC, destination MAC, protocol and TTL
questions.option_c: Source IP, destination IP, sequence number and acknowledgment number
questions.option_d: Source port, destination port, subnet mask and gateway
questions.explanation: The four-tuple consists of source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port.

questions.question: A browser opens multiple connections to the same web server. Why can the server distinguish these connections?
questions.option_a: Each browser tab uses a different destination IP address
questions.option_b: Each tab uses a different TCP version
questions.option_c: The server assigns a different MAC address to every tab
questions.option_d: Different source ports allow the connections to have distinct four-tuples
questions.explanation: Different source ports distinguish simultaneous connections to the same destination when considered with the other four-tuple values.

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of the TCP three-way handshake?
questions.option_a: ACK, SYN, FIN
questions.option_b: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
questions.option_c: SYN, FIN, ACK
questions.option_d: SYN-ACK, ACK, SYN
questions.explanation: The client sends SYN, the server responds with SYN-ACK, and the client completes the handshake with ACK.

questions.question: What information does the client communicate through its initial SYN?
questions.option_a: Its final acknowledgment number
questions.option_b: Its encryption password
questions.option_c: Its initial sequence number
questions.option_d: Its final connection termination time
questions.explanation: The initial SYN carries the client's initial sequence number, which is used to synchronize TCP communication.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the SYN-ACK message?
questions.option_a: To acknowledge the client's initial sequence number and communicate the server's own initial sequence number
questions.option_b: To terminate the connection
questions.option_c: To allocate the client's IP address
questions.option_d: To confirm that all application data has been received
questions.explanation: The server acknowledges the client's SYN and sends its own initial sequence number in the SYN-ACK.

questions.question: At which point does the server receive confirmation that the client has received its SYN-ACK?
questions.option_a: When the initial SYN arrives
questions.option_b: When the server transmits SYN-ACK
questions.option_c: When the client sends FIN
questions.option_d: When the final ACK arrives
questions.explanation: The final ACK acknowledges the server's sequence number and completes the three-way handshake.

questions.question: What resource does the server reserve when it receives an initial SYN?
questions.option_a: A fully established application session with all working buffers
questions.option_b: A half-open backlog entry holding connection state, including a Transmission Control Block
questions.option_c: A permanent destination IP address
questions.option_d: A dedicated physical network interface
questions.explanation: The server creates a half-open connection entry containing state information before it has verified that the client is genuine.

questions.question: When does a TCP connection move from the half-open backlog into the established connection table?
questions.option_a: Immediately after receiving SYN
questions.option_b: Immediately after transmitting SYN-ACK
questions.option_c: After receiving the final ACK
questions.option_d: After receiving the first FIN
questions.explanation: The final ACK completes the handshake. The server then moves the connection into its established connection table and allocates the required working buffers.

questions.question: What is the typical TCP connection termination sequence?
questions.option_a: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK
questions.option_b: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
questions.option_c: RST, SYN, FIN, ACK
questions.option_d: ACK, ACK, FIN
questions.explanation: A typical close involves FIN, acknowledgment of that FIN, the other side's FIN, and a final ACK.

questions.question: Why can TCP connection termination sometimes appear to involve only three packets?
questions.option_a: TCP skips the acknowledgment of the first FIN
questions.option_b: The second endpoint is not required to close its connection
questions.option_c: TCP replaces FIN with SYN
questions.option_d: The middle ACK and FIN can be combined into one FIN-ACK
questions.explanation: If the receiving side has nothing more to send, it can acknowledge the first FIN and send its own FIN together.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the TCP TIME_WAIT state?
questions.option_a: To keep a connection permanently open
questions.option_b: To retain connection resources temporarily so delayed duplicate segments do not interfere with future connections
questions.option_c: To retransmit every previously acknowledged segment
questions.option_d: To prevent all new connections from being established
questions.explanation: TIME_WAIT allows delayed duplicate segments to expire before the connection's resources are fully released.

questions.question: Which category best describes TCP port scanning?
questions.option_a: Connection resource exhaustion
questions.option_b: Cryptographic compromise
questions.option_c: Information gathering
questions.option_d: Physical-layer disruption
questions.explanation: TCP port scanning is reconnaissance used to discover which services are open, closed or filtered.

questions.question: What response does a typical open TCP port send after receiving a SYN scan probe?
questions.option_a: SYN-ACK
questions.option_b: FIN-ACK
questions.option_c: ICMP Echo Reply
questions.option_d: DHCP Offer
questions.explanation: An open TCP port typically responds to a SYN with SYN-ACK, indicating that a service is listening.

questions.question: What response does a typical closed TCP port send after receiving a SYN probe?
questions.option_a: SYN-ACK
questions.option_b: FIN
questions.option_c: ICMP Echo Reply
questions.option_d: RST
questions.explanation: A closed TCP port typically responds with RST to indicate that no service is listening.

questions.question: How does a SYN scan differ from a TCP connect scan?
questions.option_a: A SYN scan uses UDP while a connect scan uses TCP
questions.option_b: A SYN scan does not complete the handshake, while a connect scan completes the full handshake
questions.option_c: A connect scan never communicates with the target
questions.option_d: A SYN scan requires an established application session
questions.explanation: A SYN scan reads the initial response without completing the handshake, whereas a connect scan establishes the complete TCP connection.

questions.question: Why might an attacker prefer a SYN scan over a connect scan?
questions.option_a: It guarantees that the target cannot detect the scan
questions.option_b: It encrypts all reconnaissance traffic
questions.option_c: It avoids completing the full handshake and is generally less likely to create full connection logs
questions.option_d: It bypasses every type of firewall
questions.explanation: A SYN scan does not complete the handshake, making it quieter than a full connect scan, although it is not guaranteed to be undetectable.

questions.question: Which statement about TCP connect scans is correct?
questions.option_a: They complete the full TCP handshake and do not require special privileges in the way raw SYN scanning often does
questions.option_b: They send only malformed TCP packets
questions.option_c: They never establish a connection
questions.option_d: They rely exclusively on ICMP Port Unreachable messages
questions.explanation: A connect scan uses the normal TCP connection-establishment process and is generally more detectable than a SYN scan.

questions.question: What is the purpose of FIN, Xmas and NULL scans?
questions.option_a: To establish encrypted TCP sessions
questions.option_b: To flood a server's connection backlog
questions.option_c: To identify the physical location of a server
questions.option_d: To infer port states by sending unusual TCP flag combinations
questions.explanation: These scans exploit differences in how operating systems respond to unusual TCP flag combinations.

questions.question: In the scan behavior described in the lecture, what response is expected from a closed port receiving an unusual FIN, Xmas or NULL probe?
questions.option_a: SYN-ACK
questions.option_b: RST
questions.option_c: FIN-ACK
questions.option_d: DHCP ACK
questions.explanation: A closed port should respond with RST, while many operating systems simply drop these unusual probes when the port is open.

questions.question: Why can FIN, Xmas and NULL scans sometimes evade a firewall that primarily watches for SYN packets?
questions.option_a: They change the destination IP address automatically
questions.option_b: They use an encrypted handshake
questions.option_c: They use unusual flag combinations rather than conventional SYN probes
questions.option_d: They disable the target's TCP stack
questions.explanation: A firewall rule focused on SYN traffic may fail to identify unusual TCP flag combinations used by these scanning techniques.

questions.question: What does a TCP host sweep attempt to discover?
questions.option_a: Which hosts in an IP address range are alive and reachable
questions.option_b: Which files are stored on a server
questions.option_c: Which encryption keys are installed
questions.option_d: Which users are currently logged in
questions.explanation: A host sweep checks a range of addresses to identify active hosts rather than discovering every open port on one host.

questions.question: Which technique is commonly used in a TCP host sweep?
questions.option_a: Sending a different FIN packet to every application process
questions.option_b: Establishing a complete connection to every port
questions.option_c: Sending ICMP Timestamp Requests exclusively
questions.option_d: Sending SYN probes to the same commonly used port across an address range
questions.explanation: A TCP host sweep commonly sends SYN probes to one port across multiple destination addresses.

questions.question: Why can a TCP host sweep identify active hosts even when ICMP Echo Requests are blocked?
questions.option_a: TCP automatically converts SYN packets into ICMP messages
questions.option_b: A host may respond to TCP probes with SYN-ACK or RST independently of ICMP Echo
questions.option_c: Blocking ICMP disables TCP filtering
questions.option_d: TCP host sweeps use DNS exclusively
questions.explanation: An active host can respond to a TCP probe on an open or closed port, allowing reconnaissance without ICMP Echo.

questions.question: Which mitigation is particularly useful against TCP host sweeps across an internal network?
questions.option_a: Disabling all TCP sequence numbers
questions.option_b: Increasing the UDP header size
questions.option_c: Network segmentation
questions.option_d: Removing all IP addresses
questions.explanation: Network segmentation limits the address space that a compromised system can reach, reducing the impact of horizontal reconnaissance.

questions.question: What does OS fingerprinting attempt to identify?
questions.option_a: The operating system and version running on a target
questions.option_b: The physical MAC address of every router
questions.option_c: The user's application password
questions.option_d: The encryption key used by a VPN
questions.explanation: OS fingerprinting analyzes network-stack behavior to infer the operating system and potentially its version.

questions.question: Which combination of characteristics can help an attacker perform OS fingerprinting?
questions.option_a: File permissions and database schemas
questions.option_b: Usernames and application passwords
questions.option_c: DNS record expiration and browser cookies
questions.option_d: Default TTL, TCP window size, TCP options ordering and responses to unusual packets
questions.explanation: Different operating systems exhibit characteristic TCP/IP stack behaviors that can be compared against known fingerprints.

questions.question: Why is identifying a target's operating system valuable to an attacker?
questions.option_a: It automatically provides administrator privileges
questions.option_b: It helps the attacker identify vulnerabilities associated with that operating system and version
questions.option_c: It disables the target's firewall
questions.option_d: It reveals the target's complete source code
questions.explanation: Knowing the OS and version helps attackers select vulnerabilities and techniques relevant to the target.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what is the most important mitigation against OS fingerprinting leading to compromise?
questions.option_a: Disabling every network protocol
questions.option_b: Increasing the TCP minimum header size
questions.option_c: Keeping systems patched
questions.option_d: Disabling all application services permanently
questions.explanation: Patching ensures that identifying a particular operating system does not automatically give an attacker an exploitable known vulnerability.

questions.question: What is the central vulnerability exploited by TCP session hijacking?
questions.option_a: TCP tracks session state using sequence numbers without cryptographically authenticating subsequent packets
questions.option_b: TCP does not use port numbers
questions.option_c: TCP automatically encrypts all application data
questions.option_d: TCP cannot detect packet loss
questions.explanation: TCP sequence numbers track session state, but TCP itself does not cryptographically verify that later packets genuinely originate from the legitimate endpoint.

questions.question: What does an attacker need to inject a forged packet into an established TCP session successfully?
questions.option_a: The target's physical MAC address only
questions.option_b: The server's DNS cache
questions.option_c: The client's operating system installation media
questions.option_d: A valid current sequence number and a packet that the receiver accepts as part of the session
questions.explanation: The attacker needs appropriate sequence-number information to make the receiver accept the injected packet as valid session traffic.

questions.question: Which technique can help an attacker obtain the sequence numbers needed for TCP hijacking?
questions.option_a: Reading the target's routing table through DNS
questions.option_b: Sniffing traffic on a shared or compromised network segment
questions.option_c: Sending DHCP Discover messages
questions.option_d: Changing the target's subnet mask
questions.explanation: An attacker who can observe traffic on a shared or compromised network segment may learn the current sequence-number information.

questions.question: Why did predictable initial TCP sequence numbers historically make session hijacking easier?
questions.option_a: They allowed attackers to bypass all IP routing
questions.option_b: They eliminated the need for TCP ports
questions.option_c: Attackers could predict sequence numbers and construct acceptable forged packets
questions.option_d: They forced every connection to use UDP
questions.explanation: Predictable sequence-number generation made it easier to guess the state expected by the receiver. Modern operating systems randomize initial sequence numbers.

questions.question: Which mitigation protects TCP sessions against injected packets that lack the required cryptographic authentication?
questions.option_a: TLS encryption and authentication
questions.option_b: Increasing the server's backlog
questions.option_c: Blocking all DNS responses
questions.option_d: Reducing the UDP header size
questions.explanation: TLS protects the session's application data through cryptographic authentication and integrity checks, preventing unauthenticated injected content from being accepted as valid protected data.

questions.question: What distinguishes TCP RST injection from TCP session hijacking?
questions.option_a: RST injection targets only UDP connections
questions.option_b: RST injection establishes a new TCP connection
questions.option_c: Session hijacking only changes a destination port
questions.option_d: RST injection attempts to terminate an existing connection, while hijacking aims to take over the session or inject content
questions.explanation: Both attacks exploit insufficient authentication of TCP state, but their objectives differ: one terminates a connection, while the other takes it over.

questions.question: What type of packet does an attacker forge during a TCP RST injection attack?
questions.option_a: SYN
questions.option_b: RST
questions.option_c: FIN
questions.option_d: DHCP ACK
questions.explanation: The attacker forges a TCP Reset packet to terminate an existing connection prematurely.

questions.question: What must a forged TCP RST packet satisfy to be accepted by the receiver according to the lecture?
questions.option_a: It must contain a valid DNS response
questions.option_b: It must use a larger UDP payload
questions.option_c: Its sequence number must fall within the receiver's current valid sequence-number window
questions.option_d: It must contain a valid ICMP Echo identifier
questions.explanation: The receiver accepts a RST packet when its sequence number falls within the current valid sequence-number window.

questions.question: What is a limitation of TLS as a defense against TCP RST injection?
questions.option_a: TLS protects session content, but the underlying TCP connection may still be reset by a valid forged RST
questions.option_b: TLS disables all TCP acknowledgments
questions.option_c: TLS makes TCP use UDP
questions.option_d: TLS automatically prevents every network-layer denial-of-service attack
questions.explanation: TLS protects application data, but it does not prevent the underlying TCP connection from being terminated by a forged RST accepted by TCP.

questions.question: Which application-level capability can help recover from a TCP connection terminated by RST injection?
questions.option_a: Disabling the operating system's network stack
questions.option_b: Increasing the UDP header length
questions.option_c: Removing the application's IP address
questions.option_d: Automatic reconnection logic
questions.explanation: Applications that need resilience can implement automatic reconnection logic above TCP to recover from unexpected connection termination.

questions.question: What is the primary target of a TCP SYN flood?
questions.option_a: The target's DNS database
questions.option_b: The server's half-open connection backlog
questions.option_c: The client's browser cache
questions.option_d: The destination's routing table
questions.explanation: A SYN flood exploits the resources reserved for connections that have received SYN but have not completed the handshake.

questions.question: What happens to a server when it receives a SYN during normal TCP connection establishment?
questions.option_a: It immediately establishes a fully authenticated application session
questions.option_b: It permanently reserves all available memory
questions.option_c: It creates a half-open connection entry and sends SYN-ACK
questions.option_d: It terminates all existing TCP connections
questions.explanation: The server reserves a half-open backlog entry before receiving confirmation that the client is genuine.

questions.question: Why are spoofed source IP addresses useful in a SYN flood?
questions.option_a: They can cause SYN-ACK responses to be sent to unrelated or unreachable addresses, preventing completion of the handshake
questions.option_b: They automatically increase the server's backlog
questions.option_c: They encrypt the SYN packets
questions.option_d: They make the server complete the handshake immediately
questions.explanation: Spoofed addresses prevent the server's SYN-ACK from reaching the actual attacker in many cases, so the final ACK never arrives and half-open entries remain until timeout.

questions.question: What is the likely consequence when a SYN flood fills the server's half-open backlog?
questions.option_a: All existing connections are immediately encrypted
questions.option_b: The server changes all TCP ports to UDP
questions.option_c: The server automatically increases its network bandwidth
questions.option_d: The server becomes unable to accept new connections normally
questions.explanation: When the backlog is full, new legitimate connection attempts may be denied. Existing established connections are typically unaffected.

questions.question: Which defense is specifically designed to reduce the resource-reservation weakness exploited by SYN floods?
questions.option_a: OS fingerprinting
questions.option_b: SYN cookies
questions.option_c: UDP port scanning
questions.option_d: TIME_WAIT expansion
questions.explanation: SYN cookies encode the information needed to reconstruct connection state into the SYN-ACK sequence number, delaying allocation of real connection resources until the final ACK arrives.

questions.question: How do SYN cookies differ from simply increasing the backlog size?
questions.option_a: SYN cookies increase the physical network interface speed
questions.option_b: Increasing the backlog removes the need for a handshake
questions.option_c: SYN cookies avoid allocating normal backlog state for every initial SYN, while increasing backlog only increases available capacity
questions.option_d: Both methods completely eliminate the underlying resource-reservation asymmetry
questions.explanation: SYN cookies address the underlying resource asymmetry by delaying real allocation. A larger backlog only allows more half-open entries before exhaustion.

questions.question: Which of the following is a supplementary mitigation for SYN floods rather than a complete removal of the underlying weakness?
questions.option_a: Increasing the backlog size
questions.option_b: Replacing TCP with DNS
questions.option_c: Disabling all sequence numbers
questions.option_d: Removing all server ports
questions.explanation: Increasing backlog capacity raises the amount of traffic required to exhaust resources but does not eliminate the underlying weakness.

questions.question: What is the purpose of reducing the SYN-RECEIVED timeout during a SYN flood?
questions.option_a: To make established connections terminate immediately
questions.option_b: To disable the TCP checksum
questions.option_c: To increase the number of application processes
questions.option_d: To release abandoned half-open connection entries sooner
questions.explanation: A shorter timeout reduces the time that incomplete connections occupy backlog resources, although it does not remove the underlying vulnerability.

questions.question: Which defense is most appropriate when a SYN flood exceeds the capacity of a single organization's on-site network equipment?
questions.option_a: Increasing browser cache size
questions.option_b: Dedicated DDoS protection services
questions.option_c: Disabling TCP checksums
questions.option_d: Using only local password policies
questions.explanation: Dedicated DDoS protection services can absorb traffic volumes that an individual server or on-site firewall cannot handle.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes UDP?
questions.option_a: It requires a three-way handshake before every transmission
questions.option_b: It guarantees ordered delivery
questions.option_c: It is connectionless and maintains no protocol-level connection state
questions.option_d: It automatically retransmits every lost packet
questions.explanation: UDP sends datagrams without connection establishment and does not maintain TCP-style connection state.

questions.question: Which feature is absent from UDP according to the lecture?
questions.option_a: A checksum field
questions.option_b: Source and destination ports
questions.option_c: A transport-layer header
questions.option_d: Built-in reliability and retransmission
questions.explanation: UDP has a checksum and port fields but does not provide built-in reliability or automatic retransmission.

questions.question: What happens when UDP datagrams arrive out of order?
questions.option_a: UDP automatically rearranges them using TCP sequence numbers
questions.option_b: UDP itself does not guarantee their ordering
questions.option_c: The receiver always retransmits all datagrams
questions.option_d: The sender is automatically disconnected
questions.explanation: UDP provides no built-in ordering guarantee. If ordering is needed, the application must implement it.

questions.question: Why can UDP be cheaper for latency-sensitive applications?
questions.option_a: It eliminates all network-layer processing
questions.option_b: It guarantees that packets never get lost
questions.option_c: It avoids connection establishment and has a smaller header
questions.option_d: It encrypts packets without additional processing
questions.explanation: UDP has no handshake and an 8-byte header, reducing overhead for applications such as VoIP, gaming and video.

questions.question: Which statement about UDP application state is correct?
questions.option_a: If an application needs to track a conversation, it must implement that logic itself
questions.option_b: UDP automatically stores every connection in a Transmission Control Block
questions.option_c: UDP uses the TCP half-open backlog
questions.option_d: UDP guarantees that each datagram belongs to a previously established connection
questions.explanation: UDP itself maintains no connection state, so any required conversation tracking must be implemented by the application.

questions.question: Which of the following lists all four UDP-based attacks identified in the lecture?
questions.option_a: SYN flood, RST injection, TCP hijacking and UDP flood
questions.option_b: DNS poisoning, ARP spoofing, UDP flood and session hijacking
questions.option_c: TCP port scan, UDP host sweep, SYN flood and UDP bomb
questions.option_d: UDP port scan, UDP host sweep, UDP bomb attack and UDP flood
questions.explanation: The four UDP attacks covered are UDP port scans, UDP host sweeps, UDP bomb attacks and UDP floods.

questions.question: Why is UDP port scanning inherently more ambiguous than TCP port scanning?
questions.option_a: UDP uses encrypted headers
questions.option_b: An open UDP port may remain silent, while a closed port typically generates ICMP Port Unreachable
questions.option_c: UDP ports cannot be identified
questions.option_d: Every UDP packet requires a SYN-ACK response
questions.explanation: UDP has no handshake. Silence may indicate an open service, a filtered packet or a lost probe, making port-state identification difficult.

questions.question: What does an ICMP Port Unreachable response usually indicate during UDP port scanning?
questions.option_a: The UDP port is definitely open
questions.option_b: The host is using TCP
questions.option_c: The probed UDP port is closed
questions.option_d: The target has completed a TCP handshake
questions.explanation: A closed UDP port typically generates an ICMP Port Unreachable response.

questions.question: During UDP port scanning, what does receiving no response from the target indicate?
questions.option_a: The port is definitely open
questions.option_b: The target is definitely offline
questions.option_c: The target has accepted an authenticated connection
questions.option_d: The port may be open, or the probe or response may have been filtered or lost
questions.explanation: UDP silence is ambiguous. A port may be open without responding, but filtering or packet loss can produce the same result.

questions.question: Why might an attacker send a real DNS query to UDP port 53 during reconnaissance?
questions.option_a: To obtain a service-specific response that helps determine whether the UDP service is open
questions.option_b: To complete a TCP three-way handshake
questions.option_c: To force the target into TIME_WAIT
questions.option_d: To disable ICMP Port Unreachable messages
questions.explanation: A valid application-specific payload may cause a listening DNS service to respond, reducing the ambiguity caused by silent UDP ports.

questions.question: Which mitigation directly reduces the usefulness of ICMP Port Unreachable responses to UDP scanners?
questions.option_a: Increasing TCP receive windows
questions.option_b: Rate-limiting ICMP Port Unreachable generation
questions.option_c: Enabling TCP TIME_WAIT
questions.option_d: Increasing UDP header size
questions.explanation: Rate-limiting ICMP Port Unreachable responses reduces the scanner's clearest signal for identifying closed UDP ports.

questions.question: What is a UDP host sweep designed to discover?
questions.option_a: The exact operating system version of every host
questions.option_b: The encryption algorithm used by every service
questions.option_c: Which hosts are alive across an address range
questions.option_d: Which TCP connections are in TIME_WAIT
questions.explanation: A UDP host sweep probes multiple IP addresses to determine which hosts are active.

questions.question: How can a host reveal its existence during a UDP host sweep?
questions.option_a: By responding with a UDP service response or an ICMP Port Unreachable message
questions.option_b: By sending a TCP SYN-ACK for every UDP datagram
questions.option_c: By automatically assigning the scanner an IP address
questions.option_d: By transmitting its complete routing table
questions.explanation: A live host may respond through an active UDP service or generate ICMP Port Unreachable when the destination port is closed.

questions.question: Why is completely disabling ICMP not a sufficient defense against Layer 4 reconnaissance?
questions.option_a: TCP automatically disables all firewalls when ICMP is blocked
questions.option_b: ICMP filtering increases UDP header size
questions.option_c: All reconnaissance requires ICMP Echo Requests
questions.option_d: TCP host sweeps can use SYN probes, and UDP services may still respond through application traffic
questions.explanation: TCP host sweeps can identify hosts through SYN-ACK or RST responses, while UDP services may respond independently of ICMP Echo.

questions.question: What is the vulnerability exploited by a UDP bomb attack?
questions.option_a: Predictable TCP initial sequence numbers
questions.option_b: Insufficient validation of malformed UDP header fields by vulnerable network stacks
questions.option_c: An excessively large TCP backlog
questions.option_d: Incorrect DNS domain ownership
questions.explanation: A UDP bomb exploits implementations that fail to validate fields such as the UDP length field correctly.

questions.question: Which UDP header field is specifically mentioned in the lecture as an example of malformed packet construction?
questions.option_a: Destination MAC address
questions.option_b: TCP acknowledgment number
questions.option_c: UDP length field
questions.option_d: IP default gateway
questions.explanation: The lecture describes a malformed UDP packet whose length field does not match the actual payload size.

questions.question: What is the potential impact of a successful UDP bomb attack?
questions.option_a: Crashing or destabilizing a vulnerable network stack
questions.option_b: Automatically completing a TCP handshake
questions.option_c: Increasing the server's backlog capacity
questions.option_d: Encrypting all network traffic
questions.explanation: A malformed UDP packet may cause a vulnerable network stack to crash or become unstable, resulting in denial of service.

questions.question: Which defense is particularly important against UDP bomb attacks targeting embedded and IoT devices?
questions.option_a: Disabling all application-layer protocols
questions.option_b: Increasing the number of TCP ports
questions.option_c: Enabling TIME_WAIT on every UDP socket
questions.option_d: Keeping operating systems and device firmware patched
questions.explanation: Unpatched embedded and IoT devices may retain legacy network-stack vulnerabilities, making firmware updates especially important.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of firewall and IPS packet validation against UDP bombs?
questions.option_a: To increase the attacker's available bandwidth
questions.option_b: To reject malformed UDP packets before they reach vulnerable systems
questions.option_c: To convert UDP into TCP
questions.option_d: To establish a connection before every datagram
questions.explanation: Packet validation can identify and drop malformed UDP packets at the network boundary before they reach vulnerable hosts.

questions.question: What is the main target of a UDP flood?
questions.option_a: The TCP connection sequence number
questions.option_b: The DNS root zone
questions.option_c: The target's bandwidth and processing capacity
questions.option_d: The TCP half-open backlog exclusively
questions.explanation: UDP floods send large volumes of datagrams to exhaust network bandwidth or the target's processing resources.

questions.question: Why can an attacker start a UDP flood without establishing a connection?
questions.option_a: UDP has no connection-establishment handshake
questions.option_b: UDP requires a valid TCP session
questions.option_c: UDP automatically authenticates every sender
questions.option_d: UDP uses a three-way handshake internally
questions.explanation: UDP is connectionless, allowing attackers to transmit datagrams without completing a connection-establishment process.

questions.question: Why can UDP flooding be cheaper for an attacker than an equivalent TCP-based connection flood?
questions.option_a: UDP automatically compresses attack traffic
questions.option_b: UDP guarantees that every packet reaches the target
questions.option_c: UDP uses a larger header and requires more state
questions.option_d: UDP avoids handshake requirements and has no built-in congestion control
questions.explanation: UDP allows immediate datagram transmission without establishing connections, and it does not provide built-in congestion control.

questions.question: What secondary resource-consumption effect can occur during a UDP flood targeting closed ports?
questions.option_a: The server automatically creates TCP sessions
questions.option_b: The victim may generate ICMP Port Unreachable messages for incoming datagrams
questions.option_c: The victim's operating system changes to UDP-only mode
questions.option_d: Every datagram is converted into a DNS query
questions.explanation: When packets target closed UDP ports, the victim may generate ICMP Port Unreachable messages, creating additional processing overhead.

questions.question: Which combination is most appropriate for mitigating UDP floods?
questions.option_a: Increase TCP TIME_WAIT and enable OS fingerprinting
questions.option_b: Disable all application authentication and increase the UDP header
questions.option_c: Rate-limit UDP traffic, close unnecessary UDP ports and rate-limit ICMP Port Unreachable generation
questions.option_d: Increase the TCP initial sequence number
questions.explanation: UDP flood mitigation includes perimeter rate-limiting, closing unnecessary UDP ports and reducing secondary ICMP processing.

questions.question: What is UDP amplification in the context of large-scale DDoS attacks?
questions.option_a: Using application protocols that return much larger responses than the original requests to amplify traffic toward a victim
questions.option_b: Increasing the UDP header from 8 bytes to 20 bytes
questions.option_c: Combining two TCP handshakes into one
questions.option_d: Using SYN cookies to allocate additional UDP connections
questions.explanation: Amplification exploits UDP-based application protocols that produce responses much larger than requests, allowing attackers to increase the traffic directed at victims.

questions.question: Which protocols are given as examples of UDP-based amplification attacks in the lecture?
questions.option_a: HTTP, HTTPS and FTP
questions.option_b: SSH, Telnet and SMTP
questions.option_c: ARP, Ethernet and VLAN
questions.option_d: DNS, NTP and memcached
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies DNS, NTP and memcached as examples of application protocols that can be abused for UDP amplification.

questions.question: Which statement best explains the common underlying design assumption behind TCP and UDP vulnerabilities?
questions.option_a: Both protocols assume that every packet is encrypted
questions.option_b: The transport layer was designed with an assumption of a trusted network, providing limited sender verification by default
questions.option_c: Both protocols require application authentication before transmitting packets
questions.option_d: Both protocols were designed to prevent all denial-of-service attacks
questions.explanation: The lecture explains that Layer 4 was designed with a trusted-network assumption, resulting in minimal or absent verification at the transport layer.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes the principal TCP and UDP security weaknesses?
questions.option_a: TCP has no ports, while UDP has no checksum
questions.option_b: TCP is always encrypted, while UDP is always authenticated
questions.option_c: TCP has predictable, unauthenticated connection state, while UDP has no protocol-level connection state or sender verification
questions.option_d: TCP only suffers from amplification, while UDP only suffers from session hijacking
questions.explanation: TCP's weakness concerns its unauthenticated sequence-number-based state and premature resource allocation. UDP's weakness comes from its lack of connection state and verification.

questions.question: Why is source IP spoofing a recurring factor in many Layer 4 attacks?
questions.option_a: Layer 4 itself does not cryptographically verify the true origin of packets
questions.option_b: TCP and UDP automatically encrypt source IP addresses
questions.option_c: IP addresses cannot be used by routers
questions.option_d: Port numbers always reveal the physical identity of a sender
questions.explanation: Layer 4 does not independently authenticate the source of incoming traffic. Filtering and authentication must be provided by other layers or systems.

questions.question: Which security mechanism can help address spoofed source addresses at network boundaries?
questions.option_a: Increasing TIME_WAIT duration
questions.option_b: Changing TCP port numbers randomly
questions.option_c: Disabling TCP checksums
questions.option_d: Ingress and egress filtering
questions.explanation: Ingress and egress filtering can reduce the ability of attackers to send packets with forged source addresses.

questions.question: A company disables ICMP Echo Requests, believing this completely prevents host discovery. An attacker sends SYN probes to TCP port 80 across the company's address range. Active systems respond with SYN-ACK or RST. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.option_a: The attack cannot work because TCP requires ICMP Echo
questions.option_b: The attacker is performing a TCP host sweep, which can bypass defenses relying exclusively on ICMP Echo filtering
questions.option_c: The attacker is performing a UDP bomb attack
questions.option_d: The attacker is performing a TCP RST injection attack
questions.explanation: TCP host sweeps identify active hosts through TCP responses. Blocking ICMP Echo alone does not prevent this form of reconnaissance.

questions.question: A security analyst observes a large number of SYN packets arriving at a server. Many apparent source addresses never complete the handshake, and legitimate new connections begin failing. Which explanation best fits the evidence?
questions.option_a: An OS fingerprinting attack has modified the TCP window size
questions.option_b: A UDP port scan has exhausted the DNS cache
questions.option_c: A TCP SYN flood has exhausted the half-open connection backlog
questions.option_d: A TCP FIN scan has terminated every established session
questions.explanation: The incomplete handshakes consume half-open backlog entries. When these entries accumulate, the server may be unable to accept new legitimate connections.

questions.question: A server has a half-open backlog capacity of 500 entries. An attacker sends 700 SYN packets using spoofed source addresses. Assume the entries do not expire during the attack. What is the most likely outcome?
questions.option_a: The backlog becomes exhausted, and new connection attempts may be denied
questions.option_b: All 700 connections become fully established automatically
questions.option_c: The server automatically increases its backlog to 700
questions.option_d: Only UDP traffic is affected
questions.explanation: The first 500 incomplete connection attempts can occupy the available backlog. Additional attempts arrive when the resource is already exhausted.

questions.question: A network administrator enables SYN cookies but does not increase the backlog size. Why can this still significantly improve protection?
questions.option_a: SYN cookies encrypt all application data
questions.option_b: SYN cookies block all SYN packets
questions.option_c: SYN cookies prevent all UDP floods
questions.option_d: SYN cookies allow the server to avoid normal backlog allocation for incomplete connections until the final ACK is received
questions.explanation: SYN cookies encode connection information in the SYN-ACK sequence number and defer normal resource allocation until the client proves reachability with the final ACK.

questions.question: An attacker sends a crafted TCP packet to an established session. The receiver accepts it because its sequence number is valid. The attacker wants to inject application data. Which attack is being performed?
questions.option_a: TCP SYN flood
questions.option_b: TCP session hijacking
questions.option_c: TCP host sweep
questions.option_d: TCP port scan
questions.explanation: TCP hijacking involves injecting traffic into an existing session by exploiting the lack of cryptographic authentication of TCP packets.

questions.question: An attacker has the same sequence-number information used in TCP hijacking but sends a forged RST packet instead of application data. What is the attack's primary objective?
questions.option_a: Discovering open UDP ports
questions.option_b: Establishing an additional TCP connection
questions.option_c: Prematurely terminating a specific existing TCP connection
questions.option_d: Increasing the victim's connection backlog
questions.explanation: RST injection uses a forged Reset packet to terminate a specific existing connection rather than taking over the session to inject application content.

questions.question: A company deploys TLS to protect application traffic. An attacker can still inject a valid TCP RST packet into the underlying connection. Which assessment is most accurate?
questions.option_a: TLS prevents the attacker from reading or modifying protected content, but the connection can still be terminated at the TCP level
questions.option_b: TLS guarantees that no TCP packet can be reset
questions.option_c: TLS disables TCP sequence numbers
questions.option_d: TLS converts the connection into UDP
questions.explanation: TLS protects the session content and its integrity, but TCP connection termination remains a separate transport-layer operation.

questions.question: A scanner sends UDP probes to 100 ports. Some ports return ICMP Port Unreachable, while others remain silent. Which interpretation is the most accurate?
questions.option_a: Every silent port is confirmed open
questions.option_b: Every ICMP response indicates an open port
questions.option_c: Every silent port belongs to an offline host
questions.option_d: ICMP Port Unreachable indicates closed ports, while silence remains ambiguous
questions.explanation: UDP port scanning is inherently ambiguous because open services may not respond and filtering or packet loss can also produce silence.

questions.question: A company blocks ICMP Echo Requests and rate-limits ICMP Port Unreachable messages. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
questions.option_a: All TCP and UDP reconnaissance is now impossible
questions.option_b: These controls reduce some reconnaissance signals, but TCP probes and application-specific UDP responses may still reveal hosts and services
questions.option_c: The controls automatically prevent TCP session hijacking
questions.option_d: The controls eliminate the need for patch management
questions.explanation: ICMP filtering and rate-limiting reduce some discovery signals but cannot replace broader service exposure controls, segmentation and scan detection.

questions.question: A vulnerable IoT device crashes when it receives a UDP datagram whose length field is inconsistent with the actual payload. Which attack and mitigation best match this situation?
questions.option_a: TCP hijacking; enable SYN cookies
questions.option_b: UDP flood; increase TCP TIME_WAIT
questions.option_c: UDP bomb; patch the firmware and validate malformed packets at the firewall or IPS
questions.option_d: OS fingerprinting; disable DNS
questions.explanation: The malformed UDP length field identifies a UDP bomb-style attack. Patching and packet validation address the vulnerable implementation.

questions.question: A server receives a UDP flood directed at a closed port. Its CPU usage increases further because it generates ICMP Port Unreachable responses for incoming datagrams. What is the most appropriate additional mitigation?
questions.option_a: Rate-limit or disable excessive ICMP Port Unreachable generation
questions.option_b: Increase the TCP initial sequence number
questions.option_c: Enable additional TCP acknowledgments
questions.option_d: Increase the number of DNS records
questions.explanation: Limiting ICMP Port Unreachable generation removes the secondary resource drain caused by responding to large volumes of packets targeting closed UDP ports.

questions.question: A small business wants to reduce its exposure to port scans with almost no security budget. Which combination is most proportionate?
questions.option_a: Purchase expensive deep packet inspection equipment immediately
questions.option_b: Replace all computers and disable all networking
questions.option_c: Increase the number of exposed services and rely on passwords
questions.option_d: Disable unnecessary services, use existing firewall or IDS scan detection, and rate-limit connection attempts
questions.explanation: Reducing exposed services and using existing firewall or IDS capabilities provide meaningful protection without requiring expensive new infrastructure.

questions.question: A company has almost no security budget and is concerned about spoofed-source attacks. Which initial control provides useful protection at relatively low cost?
questions.option_a: Increasing TCP header size
questions.option_b: Enabling ingress and egress filtering at network boundaries
questions.option_c: Replacing all TCP services with UDP
questions.option_d: Increasing TIME_WAIT duration
questions.explanation: Ingress and egress filtering can reduce spoofed-source traffic using network configuration rather than expensive dedicated equipment.

questions.question: A company experiences port scans, host sweeps and SYN floods. Which strategy best demonstrates defense in depth?
questions.option_a: Rely exclusively on blocking ICMP Echo Requests
questions.option_b: Use TLS alone to prevent every Layer 4 attack
questions.option_c: Combine service minimization, scan detection, network segmentation, SYN cookies and appropriate rate-limiting
questions.option_d: Increase the number of listening TCP and UDP services
questions.explanation: Different attacks exploit different weaknesses, so a combination of preventive, detective and resource-protection controls is more effective than relying on one defense.

questions.question: A security team has limited funds. Which implementation order most closely follows the lecture's cost-effective mitigation strategy?
questions.option_a: Start with free controls such as disabling unnecessary services, enabling SYN cookies and filtering spoofed sources, then introduce low-cost rate-limiting and existing IDS/IPS capabilities before considering expensive dedicated protection
questions.option_b: Purchase dedicated DDoS protection before checking whether unnecessary services are exposed
questions.option_c: Install deep packet inspection equipment and ignore existing firewall capabilities
questions.option_d: Disable all TCP and UDP communication regardless of business requirements
questions.explanation: The lecture recommends starting with free configuration improvements, progressing to low-cost controls and investing in dedicated protection only when the risk justifies the expense.
